title: GC throttle causing pod-start stalls — incident retrospective
content:
Summary:

Late-night incident where a sudden increase in controller-driven pod churn triggered containerd/kubelet garbage collection work that saturated the node write path and caused kubelet api-server heartbeats and pod start operations to stall. Symptoms looked like transient 'pod Pending' + image pull stuck + container runtime CPU spikes across a subset of nodes, then brief etcd leader election timeouts.

Why this is interesting/unique:
- The primary throttle was not CPU or network but synchronous disk stalls during containerd image and snapshot GC jobs.
- The kubelet's GC heuristics kicked off concurrently with a large rollout that created short-lived pods (liveness retry loop) resulting in cumulative I/O.
- Calico CNI dataplane queues increased because pod IP lifecycle churn stressed the ipip tunnel table updates; these amplified pod start latency for pods scheduled onto already stressed nodes.

Timeline (UTC):
- 02:18: alert: pod-start-latency SLO breach (paging on-call).
- 02:20: on-call started triage; noticed spiky 95th token latency for model-hosting pods (app metric).
- 02:22: kubectl get pods showed many pods stuck in ContainerCreating or ImagePullBackOff on a handful of nodes (ip-10-4-19-*)
- 02:25: top/node-exporter showed containerd CPU jumped and disk_io_time high on those nodes.
- 02:27: dmesg on node showed several EXT4/overlayfs journal commit stalls (~500ms - 2s).
- 02:30: observation: a deployment was rolling out a new sidecar with aggressive liveness probes (30s). Restart churn >40 pods/min across cluster for a short burst.
- 02:33: attempted mitigation: cordon one of the worst nodes and drain; drain blocked on pod eviction due to timeout in preStop hooks and slow image cleanup.
- 02:37: scaled problematic deployment to 0 replicas to stop churn; pod creation rate dropped drastically.
- 02:42: manually killed containerd GC processes on three nodes (temporary mitigation) and restarted containerd on one node to clear stuck jobs.
- 02:50: pods started scheduling more normally; by 03:05 SLO back within acceptable range.

What we saw in logs (representative snippets):
- /var/log/messages:
  Oct 19 02:24 ip-10-4-19-22 kernel: INFO: task containerd:1234 blocked for more than 122 seconds.
  Oct 19 02:24 ip-10-4-19-22 kernel: buffer_flush/evict wrote 0 bytes due to IO scheduler stalls

- containerd logs:
  time="2024-10-19T02:25:11Z" level=info msg="starting garbage collection"
  time="2024-10-19T02:25:12Z" level=warning msg="gc: failed to remove snapshot x: device busy"

Key hypotheses (ordered):
1) Rapid pod churn triggered overlapping GC jobs that turned into synchronous writes and overlayfs journal pressure, causing kernel-level write stalls.
2) Kubelet GC threshold heuristics not tuned for high-churn workloads; GC runs triggered too aggressively.
3) CNI dataplane (Calico) update rate for IP lifecycle amplified scheduling latency by blocking the route programming path while kernel was saturated.
4) The rollout's liveness config created a feedback loop (crash -> restart -> new pod -> GC on old container layers) that amplified the issue.

Immediate mitigations taken (chronological):
- Scaled down the offending deployment to stop churn (02:37).
- Cordon/drain worst nodes to prevent new pods being scheduled there (02:33-02:40).
- Restarted containerd on nodes where GC was stuck (02:42).
- Increased pod eviction timeout on the drain command to allow preStop to finish (temporary).

Impact summary:
- ~18 minutes of elevated pod start latency affecting ~12 nodes; ~220 pods affected across multiple namespaces (model-serving, sidecars).
- Two brief etcd leader election events recorded (latency to control plane increased for ~15s).
- No data loss; customer-facing request error rate rose ~3% during peak.

Post-incident analysis and root cause:
- Root cause is a combination of unoptimized GC behavior on overlayfs/containerd plus application-level rollout churn from an aggressive liveness probe config. The kernel's writeback/journal behavior during overlapped GC + image pulls caused stalls on the nodes' disk subsystem (EBS gp2 observed higher latency during the window).
- Secondary factor: calico ipip program path is single-threaded per node for some operations in this kernel path; when the kernel is busy, dataplane updates queue up and add to scheduling delays.

Immediate follow-ups (actionable):
- Short-term (P0/P1):
  1) Update emergency runbook: add step to scale down suspected high-churn deployments before draining nodes. (owner: Miguel)
  2) Add a quick diagnostic checklist to on-call playbook to check containerd GC and overlayfs journal stalls (commands below). (owner: Priya)
  3) Add an alert: node.disk_io_time > 80% + containerd_cpu > 60% for 2m -> page SRE and run automated node cordon suggestions. (owner: Jonah)
- Medium-term (P2):
  4) Tweak kubelet GC thresholds for nodes with high image churn; consider deferring image garbage collection during high pod churn windows. Experiment on a staging pool. (owner: Eng-Infra)
  5) Add rate-limiting / circuit-breaker to the sidecar rollout pipeline so a bad liveness/rolling strategy cannot cause cluster-wide churn. (owner: deployment-sre)
  6) Work with Calico upstream to confirm dataplane code paths for IP lifecycle updates; evaluate whether offloading some operations or using BGP routing mode mitigates pressure. (owner: Networking)
- Long-term (P3):
  7) Investigate using overlayfs mount options and kernel tunables to reduce journal sync latency for our EBS profile. (owner: Eng-Infra)
  8) Consider an admission controller to detect extremely short-lived pods (eg <30s lifetime) and flag for manual review or impose limits on restart backoffs. (owner: Platform)

Runbook snippets / commands (notes-to-self style):
- Quick checks for on-call:
  kubectl get nodes -o wide --selector=topology.zone=us-west-2a
  sar -d 1 5  # disk stats
  pidstat -u -h 1 5 | grep containerd
  journalctl -u containerd -n 200 --no-pager
  dmesg | tail -n 200 | grep -i stall
  crictl ps -a | grep -E 'CrashLoopBackOff|ImagePullBackOff'

- If containerd GC stuck:
  systemctl restart containerd  # short-term; be aware this restarts runtime on node
  # or, to avoid immediate container restarts, find gc process and kill it carefully:
  ps aux | grep containerd | grep garbage_collect
  kill -9 <pid-of-gc> && monitor disk writeback before uncordon

Open questions / unresolved:
- Why did EBS latency spike coincide exactly with GC? Is our io profile pushing gp2 into bursting throttle? Need storage team data.
- Could kubelet be more conservative around concurrent GC vs image pulls? We should test sequentializing GC with image pull operations.
- Is the calico dataplane single-threaded for certain ipip path ops? If so, can we make route programming async and tolerant to kernel stalls?

Postmortem partners and owners (high level):
- Storage/Infra: verify EBS metrics and consider upgraded volumes or IO configuration. (owner: Samir)
- Platform/Deployment: add rollout rate-limit and safer default liveness probes. (owner: Karen)
- Networking: confirm calico behavior and plan mitigations. (owner: Miguel)
- SRE: update runbooks and alerts; staging experiments. (owner: Priya)

Notes / context snippets for next on-call:
- If you see small repeated restarts of a single sidecar type across many nodes, check image layer churn and GC schedule; scaling the deployment to 0 has been effective in stopping the GC cascade while we stabilize nodes.
- Prefer draining with --ignore-daemonsets and longer timeout flags when kernel stalls are observed to avoid making the situation worse.

Appendix: quick paste of commands used during incident (audit):
- kubectl -n model-serving scale deployment fast-sidecar --replicas=0  # stopped churn
- kubectl cordon ip-10-4-19-22 && kubectl drain ip-10-4-19-22 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data --grace-period=120
- systemctl restart containerd && journalctl -u containerd -f

Draft runbook edits suggested (to be added to CLUSTER-GC-RUNBOOK):
- Add a section: "High churn mitigation" with explicit checklist to rapidly scale down offending deployments and to avoid immediate forced drains.
- Add instrumentation: capture containerd GC run counts and durations in node exporter metrics; create dashboard.

End notes:
- This incident was contained without customer data loss, but it exposed an operational gap for high-churn workloads interacting badly with our node GC and CNI behavior.
- Next steps: schedule a runbook review session with infra + networking + platform this sprint and mark follow-ups in JIRA-SRE-4721.

---

Notes to self: when writing the final postmortem, include a small reproduction in staging (create a deployment with 20 replicas set to crash quickly with 10s liveness; run and observe overlayfs GC interactions).
